results.text:
One of the big problems with Cucumber, over the years, was the fact that the programmers wrote the fixtures, and so there was a perverse incentive for the programmers to tune the GWT syntax in a way that made the fixtures easier to write.  This led to lots of nasty implementation complexity leaking into the GWT statements. 

CLAUDE feels the same perverse incentive.  It tries to fill the GWT statements with implementation details.  However, this is easy to countermand.  When I see implementation details leaking into the GWT statements, I fire up an agent to remove them and return the statements to natural language that describes only external observables.  

You've got to stay on top of these lazy junior developers.  They'll make a horrible mess if you take the leash off them.

results.text:
Food for thought.

The fact that I am now working on some code that @esrtweet Eric Raymond worked on forty years ago is evidence that forty years ago there weren't very many programmers in the world.  

I had the same experience a few years back when I wrote a PDP-8 emulator for the iPad and got the PAL-D assembler to work.  Then I found that the PAL-D assembler was written by a very young Ed Yourdon, back in the '60s.  I was able to tweet him (it was twitter back then) that his code runs again!  He smiled.  That was the year before his passing.

There weren't a lot of us back then.  The circle of old programmers is small because the circle of young programmers was small fifty years ago.

results.text:
Consider Cucumber.  It is a generic tool that translates GIVEN/WHEN/THEN statements (among others) into code that calls a set of test fixtures written by the programmers.  Those fixtures do the hard work of translating the data in the GWT statements and calling into the guts of the system being tested.

What I have created with CLAUDE is a Parser/Generator pair that understands both a very specific GWT syntax, that is tuned to the application, and that generates test code that is fully aware of the internals of the system.  So it is a strange hybrid of Cucumber and the test fixtures.  

It took me about 8 hours to get this working, most of which was waiting for CLAUDE.  It turns out that CLAUDE struggled quite a bit, and spent a LOT of time and tokens working out the intersection between the simple GWT parsing and the much more complex system internals.

To get that intersection right required some minor modifications to the syntax of the GWT statements, and some rather more complicated changes to the internal flow of the application.  Those changes did not affect observable system behavior, but were necessary to reorder certain events and processes to adapt them to the coarse granularity of the GWT statements.

Had I started this project, six weeks ago, using GWT statements as  the driver of behavior, the process would have been much smoother, and the pain of the last week and a half could have been avoided.

Lesson learned.  And it's an old lesson indeed.  The newer things are, the more relevant the old rules become.

results.text:
OK, well, it's taken me two days but I now have a very robust acceptance test parser that generates coded tests from BDD statements.  This parser is very specific purpose.  It has deep knowledge of the internals of the system.  That means the Given/When/Then statements are not abstract or obtuse.  The parser knows what the regular english statements mean and generates the appropriate code.

Now I have a very complete set of acceptance tests that anchor the observable behavior of the system.  Next step is to add some new behavior by first writing new acceptance tests and then making them pass.  ATDD FTW.

But now it seems to have settled down and I’m actually able to write acceptance tests and they generate very quickly and they pass, which is the most important part. So I may be over the hump. We’ll see.
